1:
The commentators who describe Sardis all describe a ruin. Ellicott calls the modern Sart a mere village of paltry huts, once the capital of the old Lydian monarchy and associated with Croesus, Cyrus and Alexander, the great entrepot of dyed woollen fabrics where the art of dyeing is said to have been invented and gold-dust was found in the sand of the Pactolus, laid waste by an earthquake under Tiberius and given over to a worship of Cybele whose rites encouraged impurity. Robertson adds the two judgments that have stuck to it, Ramsay's phrase the city of Death and another's contrast of past splendour and present unresting decline. On the titles Christ takes, Ellicott notices a change from the opening vision: there he was seen holding the stars in his right hand, here he is said to have the seven Spirits and also the stars, and it is hard to overlook the unhesitating way in which he is spoken of as owning the Spirit who alone can make the angels of his Church shine. Henry draws the pastoral consequence, that to every minister and church a measure of the Spirit is given to improve, not ordinarily withdrawn until they forfeit it by misimprovement.

What the deadness consists in is the question, and the answers differ by more than emphasis. Henry describes a reputation deserved on every visible count — purity of doctrine, unity, uniformity in worship, decency and order, with no unhappy divisions on record — and locates the fault entirely in what does not fall under the observation of men: a form of godliness but not the power, and what little life remained ready to die. Barnes notices what the other letters make conspicuous by its absence, that the Saviour specifies no prevailing error or false doctrine here as at Ephesus and Thyatira, so that the complaint is a simple want of religion. Clarke makes it a matter of withdrawal, that the Spirit, having been repeatedly grieved, is about finally to depart. Bede reads the address as a rebuke of one man, the angel being the bishop, who is not diligent in correcting the bad: to thyself thou seemest to be alive, but if thou art not watchful in the correction of the wicked thou wilt be numbered among the dead; and if a ruler has not striven to incite others, though he appear guiltless before men his works are not perfect before God. Victorinus classes them as men who are careless and carry on other transactions in the world than they ought, Christians only in name, since it is not enough for a tree to live and have no fruit, nor to confess Christ without having him in our work. Ellicott alone diagnoses the mechanism: living with the credit of superior piety, it was easy to grow satisfied with the reputation, and self-satisfaction is the road to self-deception.

On the remedy they are nearer together. Ellicott renders the command become wakeful, for it will not do to rouse and sleepily grasp at one's weapons, or even to stand for once at arms. Robertson observes that Christ does not say arise from the dead, since there are vestiges of life. Henry explains the works not found filled up as an emptiness inside the form — prayers not filled up with holy desires, alms-deeds not with true charity, sabbaths not with devotion of soul — and Clarke says the same of the doers, that they performed duties of all kinds but no duty completely, constantly beginning and never bringing anything to an end. Gill hears the call to remember as addressed to his own age, taking Sardis for the church since the Reformation and the things received and heard for the doctrines of grace preached by Luther and others, now almost buried in forgetfulness — this, he says, is exactly our case.
4:
The few are counted carefully. Bede fastens on the wording, that he said not a few but a few names, for he calleth his own sheep by name and writes their names in heaven. Clarke explains the idiom from church practice, members being enrolled in a book when admitted, so that names stand for the people who bore them; and the defiled garments from Jewish usage, in which holiness is the garb of the soul and evil actions stains upon it, citing a parable of a king who gave royal garments to his servants — the prudent folded them away, the foolish wore them at their daily labour, and when the king asked for them the clean were laid up in his wardrobe and those who brought them spotted went to prison. Gill counts them a different way, not few in comparison of the world, in which sense all the elect are few, but few in comparison of the formal lifeless professors this church abounds with; for there may not only be hypocrites in churches but a majority of them. Ellicott guards the praise: the words cannot be understood of absolute purity, and what is commended is that in the deathlike self-complacent lethargy around them they had kept earnest in the pursuit of holiness. Wesley alone turns the commendation back on the man addressed: the few had not separated themselves from the rest, otherwise the angel of Sardis would not have had them; yet it was no virtue of his that they were unspotted, and his fault that they were but few.

On what the white is they divide by degree. Ellicott distinguishes two whites, the undefiled robe of the verse before and the lustrous white of glory promised here, and reports a suggested reference to the dyes for which Sardis was celebrated; Barnes takes white simply as the emblem of innocence, the reward being that those who kept their garments uncontaminated on earth should appear so clothed in heaven. On the worthiness all three qualify in the same direction. Barnes denies any claim of merit, saying only that there is a fitness in their appearing there, since they have the character to which God has promised eternal life. Henry says it is not a legal but a gospel worthiness, not merit but meetness. Robertson makes the grammatical version of the point, that they are worthy in a relative sense, not in the sense in which God and Christ are called worthy.

The promise not to blot out the name divides them more sharply, since it raises the question whether names are blotted out at all. Barnes finds a positive assurance of security: no one can have access to that book but he who keeps it, so the name will be found there on the great day and for ever, and the salvation of the redeemed is therefore secure. Ellicott reports the opposite reading, that a process of erasure is ever going on besides the process of entering, and when the soul has finally taken its choice for evil the pen is drawn through the guilty name. Wesley states it as plainly as it can be: the overcomer's name will not be blotted out like that of the angel of the church at Sardis. Henry holds the two together by dividing the enrolment: men may be enrolled in the registers of the church as baptized and professing, and such a name may be blotted out when it appears that it was but a name, such men being left of God to blot out their own names by gross and open wickedness; but the names of those that overcome shall never be blotted out. Clarke supplies the practice behind the figure: the great council stripped a faulty priest of his white garments and clothed him in black, and a citizen was struck from the register when his citizenship was forfeited.
7:
Philadelphia is the one city described with hope. Ellicott derives the name from Attalus Philadelphus, king of Pergamos, and places it on the slopes of Mount Tmolus in a district whose soil favoured the vine, with the head of Bacchus on its coins,; the region was volcanic and few cities suffered more from earthquakes, yet of all the seven it had the longest life as a Christian city, and he quotes the judgment that Philadelphia alone has been saved, a column in a scene of ruins. Robertson adds that it was rebuilt by Tiberius after the great earthquake and for a time called Neo-Caesarea, and gives Ramsay's name for it, the Missionary City. Henry takes the name for the church's character, from the brotherly love for which the citizens were eminent as a civil fraternity, and observes that no fault is found with this church, though doubtless there were faults in it of common infirmity, for love covers such faults. On the titles, Clarke says holiness essentially dwells in him and from him all holiness is derived, and he is the fountain of truth, who can neither lie nor be imposed on. Ellicott is more exact: holy carries the idea of consecration, of what is set apart to God, and true expresses more than the opposite of false, being the reality in contrast with the shadow, the antitype with the type.

The key of David draws the fullest comment. Ellicott records that some early commentators found in it the key of knowledge which the scribes had taken away, and answers that this is not wrong but too limited, only a corner of the meaning; the word David and the derivation from the prophet point wider, to Christ as the true Steward of the house of David, against whom the self-seeking stewards vainly claimed a right of exclusion from synagogue or church. Barnes is careful the other way, quoting the caution that applying the same terms to Peter and to Christ does not prove the steward in the prophet a type of Christ, but merely that the same words admit of different applications. Clarke presses the sovereignty in it: David could open or shut the kingdom of Israel to whom he pleased and was not bound to leave it even to his eldest son, and as applied here the words show Christ absolute. Henry itemises the acts of that government: he opens a door of opportunity to his churches, of utterance to his ministers, of entrance by opening the heart; and shuts heaven against the foolish virgins who have slept away their day of grace.

What the opened door is they answer differently. Barnes canvasses three senses — ability to do good, access to the heavenly palace, escape from danger and persecution — rejects the last, and takes it in the largest sense, that this church had no restraint upon it at all. Robertson takes it more narrowly as an opportunity for missionary effort in spite of the Jewish hostility, and Ellicott passes on the maxim that the reward of a little strength is a door opened. Clarke reads the little strength as little political authority or influence, and Henry hears a gentle reproof in it, that a little grace is not proportioned to so wide a door, and though Christ accepts a little strength believers should not rest satisfied in a little. On the promise that the synagogue shall come and worship at their feet, Barnes denies that conversion is necessarily meant, taking it of enemies constrained to render respect; Henry holds that they shall be convinced they were in the wrong and desire to be taken into communion; Clarke expects them to be obliged to sue to the Christians for toleration in the most abject manner; and Ellicott, who reads the promise as covering only some, expects the suspected to be transformed by time into the respected.
10:
The word of my patience they explain in the same direction. Gill takes the Gospel to be so called because it gives an account of the patience of Christ in the midst of all his outward meanness and humiliation, and because it is the means of implanting and increasing that grace in those who receive it. Henry makes the same three-fold point and adds the sequence he draws from it, that a day of gospel peace is a day of God's patience, seldom so well improved as it should be, and therefore often followed by an hour of trial. What the keeping amounts to is where they begin to differ. Ellicott states the principle first, that the one who keeps God's word is kept, and then narrows the promise: it does not mean being kept away from the tribulation but being kept out from it, the head held above the waters. Barnes narrows it further, holding that they would not be kept from calamity at all but from the temptation of apostasy in calamity, and observing that one of the highest rewards of patience in one trial is the grace to bear another, since God does not leave those who have shown that they will not leave him. Wesley reads it as plain exemption, that they should not enter into the temptation at all but it should pass over them.

What the hour of temptation was they answer by three different calendars. Clarke and Wesley both name the persecution under Trajan, and Wesley gives the reason it deserved the name of temptation rather than mere affliction: the two preceding persecutions were under the monsters Nero and Domitian, but Trajan was so admired for his goodness, and his persecution of such a nature, that it did thoroughly try them that dwelt on the earth. Barnes refuses to identify it, noting only that nothing can be determined with certainty, though he mentions the earthquake recorded by a Roman historian which sank twelve cities of Asia Minor in a single night, by which Philadelphia was deeply affected. Gill puts it in the future altogether, as a trial to come upon the reformed churches at the beginning of this period, out of which the truly godly will be delivered, antichrist destroyed, and the latter day glory brought in. Henry declines the question and states a rule instead, that when the trial is general and universal it is usually the shorter.

On the pillar two of them notice where the promise was heard. Ellicott and Robertson both observe that Philadelphia was a city of earthquakes, so that an unshaken pillar was a pointed image, and Ellicott adds that inscriptions may still be found on the sides of the marble pillars surviving among its ruins. But what the pillar does they dispute. Ellicott takes it that those who overcome will prove real supports to the great Christian temple; Henry denies exactly this, since heaven needs no such props, and makes the pillar a monument instead — one that shall never be defaced nor removed, as many stately pillars erected in honour of Roman emperors and generals have been. Robertson keeps both senses, calling the metaphor doubly significant of being firmly fixed and of giving stability to the building, and finds in the going out no more that fixity of character is at last achieved. Clarke reads the whole promise through the sanctuary: the two pillars of the temple at Jerusalem were stability and strength, and to have the name written is to be made a priest, since the priest wore Holiness to the Lord upon his forehead, while the names of the twelve tribes on the high priest's breastplate give place to the apostles of the new Jerusalem.
14:
Laodicea was rich, and they say so before anything else. Ellicott names it from Laodice, wife of the second Antiochus, notes that it shared with Thyatira and Sardis in the dye trade, its wools famous for the rich blackness of their colour, and reports the fact that tells most: when the city suffered in the great earthquake its people rebuilt without applying to the Imperial Treasury, as the neighbouring towns were compelled to do. Robertson adds the banking and the manufacture of woollen carpets, the worship of Asklepios with its medical school, and Ramsay's name for the place, the City of Compromise, observing that no praise at all is bestowed on this church. Henry, who describes a wall of vast compass, three marble theatres and a city built like Rome upon seven hills, ends where the others do not, with the ruins that lie there still as an awful monument of the wrath of the Lamb — and yet this was one of the seven golden candlesticks, for a corrupt church is still a church. On the titles, Ellicott observes that the Amen is used here alone as a personal name, the Hebrew word for verily, chosen to recall how often our Lord prefaced his own utterances with it; and that the beginning must be taken actively, not first among the created but the origination of all creation, the point needed in a church tempted to worship inferior principalities. Robertson says the same against the Arians, and Clarke that by these titles he prepares them for the humiliating truths he is about to declare.

Why cold should be preferred to lukewarm is the question, and Barnes gives three reasons. Such a state is more honest, since there is no disguise, and we know with whom we are dealing. It is more honourable, for of a man who makes professions never to be realised nothing can be made, whereas in open and earnest opposition, though wrong, there are traits which under a better direction may become elements of greatness — the character of Saul of Tarsus always had them, and that of Judas, even under the Redeemer's own teaching, never did. And there is more hope of conversion in it, the most hopeless of conditions being that of one who enters the church deceived, since he will not apply to himself the truth addressed to sinners, nor that addressed to hypocrites, and will resist as uncharitable any effort to reclaim him. Clarke reaches the same place by another road, calling them neither heathens nor Christians, too good for hell and too bad for heaven, and quoting both a couplet on being to good and evil equally bent, at once a devil and a saint, and the pagan moralist's rule that a man ought to be one kind of man, either good or bad. Henry states the principle flatly: if religion is worth anything it is worth everything, there is no room for neutrality, and an open enemy shall have fairer quarter than a perfidious neuter. Wesley alone draws a doctrine from the wish rather than a rebuke: it plainly implies that our Lord does not work on us irresistibly, as fire does on the water it heats.

The threat they explain from the stomach. Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all note that tepid water tends to sicken and provoke a vomit, the word chosen meaning rejection with extreme disgust. Gill describes the temper that earns it: a lukewarm professor serves God and mammon, halts between two opinions, cares little which religion is best, yet keeps up a round of duty and rests in the external form. Henry names the disguises it wears, since men call their lukewarmness charity, meekness, moderation and largeness of soul; it is nauseous to Christ, and makes those so who allow themselves in it. Wesley alone keeps the door open, adding that the rejection stands unless thou repent.
17:
The boast and the verdict are set side by side, and the commentators sharpen the contrast rather than soften it. Robertson observes that the church carried the pride of a wealthy city into its spiritual life, so that it was rich in pride and conceit but poor in grace and ignorant of its poverty — the reverse of Smyrna, poor in wealth and rich in grace. Ellicott takes the five words as an amplification of the reason for the rejection, calling this church the type and embodiment of wretchedness: their wealth led them into a quiet and unaggressive kind of religion, and self-complacency taught them to believe the best of themselves and then to believe in themselves. They were hypocrites who did not know they were hypocrites, and on that he quotes a passage he plainly thinks decisive: the victim of passion may be converted, and the gay and the thoughtless and the ambitious, but who is to convert the hypocrite, who cannot know he is one by the very law of his character, and the greater hypocrite he is the more sincere he must think himself. Clarke identifies the particular error behind the confidence, that they rested in what they had already received and seemed to think that once in grace must be still in grace; and he presses the first word hard, since the term rendered wretched is used of men worn out with grievous labour, as those in a stone quarry or condemned to the mines, so that instead of being heirs of the kingdom they were in the condition of the most abject slaves. Gill reads the wealth as partly literal, since riches seldom do the churches of Christ any good, and did none in the time of Constantine.

The counsel that follows is drawn from the city's own trades, and two of them say so. Robertson identifies the eye-salve as a famous Phrygian powder made at Laodicea; the gold answers to its banking and the white raiment to the black wools it sold. Ellicott hears irony in the invitation, since how could the poor and naked buy, but finds the sting drawn by the prophet's invitation to buy without money and without price. What the gold stands for they dispute. Clarke and Wesley make it faith — faith that shall stand in every trial, purified in the furnace of affliction. Barnes makes it religion at large, as the most precious of the metals stands for the most precious of possessions. Ellicott argues for love instead, since the Laodiceans were like those who had gifts and tongues and understanding and liberality but lacked the fervent love without which all is nothing, and love is the only coin which passes at heaven's mart; possession of it would bring their zeal out of the tepid into the fervent state. On the eye-salve he adds that a people proud of their enlightenment thought, like the Pharisees, that they saw, and that the anointing might be painful.

That the whole rebuke is an act of love they take from the proverb behind it. Barnes says a father recalls a disobedient child, and there is no higher proof of love than to administer, at great pain to himself, the chastening that saves him. Ellicott is precise about the two verbs: the first is the word used of the work of the Spirit and signifies to bring conviction rather than empty censure, the second signifies to educate by means of correction; and the pronoun is emphatic, calling attention to the fidelity of Christ's love against the weak partiality of human love. Robertson notes that the zeal commanded is the very word for boiling, set deliberately against their lukewarmness. Wesley makes the application personal and startled: whomsoever I love — even thee, thou poor Laodicean; O how much has his unwearied love to do.
20:
Who is at the door, and when, is the first disagreement. Gill reads the standing there as the near approach of Christ to judgment and the knocking as the notice given by the forerunners of his coming, observed by few, so general a sleepiness having seized all professors, and issuing in the midnight cry. Barnes reads it of the individual heart, drawing two things from the knocking: that he desires admittance, and that he recognises the right of the man within to open or not. He does not obtrude himself, nor employ force; if admitted he comes in and dwells, if rejected he turns quietly away, perhaps to knock again, perhaps never to come back. From the same image he takes the decisive point, that the attempt at reconciliation begins with the Saviour, who presents himself at the door as if he desired the friendship of man, salvation being never represented in the Scriptures as originated by man. Clarke agrees and puts the emphasis on the handle: the opening must be the sinner's own act, done with power received from his offended Lord, who will make no forcible entry. He supports it from two rabbinic sayings: in one God asks his children to open him a door of repentance no wider than a needle's eye and promises to open doors through which cattle may pass; in the other the doors stay shut against the man who conceals his sin before the holy King but fly open to him who confesses it. Robertson keeps both readings, calling it a picture of the Lord's advent which is true also of the individual response to his call.

The supper they take as fellowship and leave much as they find it. Robertson calls it fellowship in the Messianic kingdom and purely metaphorical; Clarke divides the promise in two, that to sup with him is to hold communion and feed him with the bread of life, and that he shall sup with Christ when brought at last to everlasting glory. The throne needs more care. Ellicott finds two thrones mentioned: Christ's own, which glorified saints are promised a share in, and the Father's, which is the power of divine majesty, wherein none may sit but God and the God-man. He also reads it as the last step of a series carrying the thought from the garden through the wilderness and the temple to the throne. Clarke does not divide the thrones but presses their identity, since Christ has conquered and is set down upon the Father's throne, and it is on that same throne that those faithful unto death are finally to sit — how astonishing this state of exaltation, and who can conceive its dignity.

Two of them end by noticing where this promise falls. Clarke observes that this is the worst of the seven churches and yet the most eminent of the promises are made to it, which shows that the worst may repent, finally conquer, and attain the highest state of glory. Ellicott makes the same observation with an eye to the despondency that follows the collapse of self-satisfied imaginations: though their religion has been proved an empty thing, the highest place is within reach of the lowest, and the faintest spark of grace may be fanned into the mightiest flame. Robertson looks back over all seven, noting that each message begins and ends alike, each is suited to the actual condition of its church, and the Shepherd lays bare the particular peril in each. Clarke closes by quoting Wesley on the arrangement: the call to hear stands before the promise in the first three letters and after it in the last four, dividing the seven in two; and the victory to which these promises are annexed is not the ordinary victory of every believer but a special victory over great and peculiar temptations, won by those strong in faith.
